title: US Supreme Court declines to hear dispute over copyrights for AI-generated material
author: IoncedreamedisuckmyD

comments.author: featherless_fiend
comments.body:
It's not news that AI works can't be copyrighted, we have articles from 3 years ago saying this. But antis keep reframing it as a new development over and over, because it's the only thing they have.

You don't even need copyright on a product in order to sell it!

The only point of copyright is so someone won't nick your shit. But no one's going to anyway because:

1. Pure AI stuff is considered worthless by the populace anyway. Why wouldn't you just prompt it yourself?

2. They have no idea how much human input was involved in the AI work, so they risk breaking the law by taking it.

replies.author: hblok
replies.body:
The second point is actually good.

It gives the AI generated works pseudo protection after all.

replies.author: TopTippityTop
replies.body: Also, the copyright determination only refers to works fully generated without any human input. With human input, it can and has been copyrighted.

replies.author: Aggressive_Finish798
replies.body: Only the human part is copywrittable. The AI generated portions are not.

replies.author: TopTippityTop
replies.body:
Not quite how it works, since they mesh so much in production. Can't pull one from the other. For example, if Im making a character, draw the gesture, let the AI fill in a little, then I define some of the design, let the AI fill....that's cooyrightable even if much of it was AI. Works using similar workflows like this have already been copyrighted.

When you're dealing with pros work, very rarely it relies solely on a prompt and a button. It's all copyrightable.

replies.author: Aggressive_Finish798
replies.body: But the basis stands. You can do all the fidleing around on top and that is probably copyrightable, but whatever the AI makes.. nope.

replies.author: TopTippityTop
replies.body: And yet, works have been copyrighted. The only ones denied were 100% a prompt + button generations. Even .ore complex workflows with controlnet but not actual manual drawings have been accepted. So long as there is human input it's fair game... And eventually even a prompt and choice of seed will be seen as human input. It's the way it'll progress.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
It's not that it can't be copyrighted it's just that you don't immediately own copyright like you would if you were to draw a picture for example.

As you say AI can be copyrighted based on how much human input was involved. Plus in different countries different laws will apply anyway.

This is all mostly irrelevant though as copyright only really helps large corporations that use it to bully smaller companies and individuals. For any normal person, whenever you put something online it's likely to be stolen and there's little you can do most of the time other than beg whatever platform it's on to remove it.

comments.author: tomqmasters
comments.body: All the circuit court ruling established is the an AI cannot hold a copyright.  The human would have been able to hold the copyright for the generated work.

replies.author: fantasstic_bet
replies.body: It also established that artwork generated through purely prompting is also not copy writable. In order for a work to be copy writable, it would need to be transformative of the AI output.

replies.author: tomqmasters
replies.body: No, actually you are referring to a statement by the copyright office, not law, and has never been tested in court.

comments.author: InsolentCoolRadio
comments.body:
This is silly.

The case is more about whether or not robots count as people.

If the court ruled that copyright worked this way, and that inanimate objects (which we’ll call “robots”) could own copyrights that would mean robots had property rights which would mean robots had rights and then I’d be charged with murder for deleting my Replika and anyone who’s ever played an action game would be accused of war crimes.

Inanimate objects don’t have rights.

When that changes … they’ll let us know.

replies.author: tomqmasters
replies.body: robots are not people, but somehow corporations are people.
